'''Volume, liquidity and depth''' are three different things that beginners read as one. Getting them apart is the difference between believing a price and being able to '''get''' that price. This page is part of the series under [[How Cryptocurrencies Gain Value]], and it is the practical answer to why a token can show a large market cap and still be untradeable.

== 1. The three measurements, and why volume is the weakest ==

* '''Spread''' — the gap between the best bid (highest anyone will pay) and the best ask (lowest anyone will sell for). A tight spread means the two sides nearly agree.
* '''Depth''' — how much is actually resting in the book within some distance of the middle. This is the one that decides whether your order fills.
* '''Slippage''' — the difference between the price you expected and the price you got. It is the consequence of the other two.

'''Trading volume is none of these.''' Volume is a count of what already happened; depth is a measure of what can happen next. A coin can report high volume and still move hard against a modest order if the book is thin at your size.<ref>https://coincraddle.com/market-cap-vs-volume-vs-liquidity-what-actually-matters</ref> All three of spread, depth and slippage can be computed from public order-book data, which means '''anyone can check them''' and nobody has to take a project's word for it.

== 2. What a thin book does to a quoted price ==

In a deep market your order is a drop in a bucket. In a thin one it ''is'' the bucket.

A large order walks the book: it fills against the best ask, then the next, then the next, each worse than the last, until it is filled.<ref>https://crypto.news/what-is-otc-trading-crypto-whales-explained/</ref> So the "price" you saw was the price of the '''last small trade''', not the price of your trade.

The Matrix page already shows this at our own scale, and it is worth repeating because it is the most honest number on this wiki: CURE has shown a best bid and best ask separated by roughly '''2,700×'''. A market cap computed from the last price there describes '''a transaction that cannot occur'''. That is not a criticism of the token — it is the gap a real market is built to close.

Useful rules of thumb from the trading literature, which are heuristics and not standards:

* An order under '''1%''' of the depth within about 1% of mid tends to fill at or near the quote; an order approaching '''100%''' of that depth consumes the visible book.<ref>https://www.ekx.io/blog/how-to-evaluate-crypto-exchange-liquidity-depth</ref>
* An order above roughly '''5%''' of nearby available volume should be expected to cause meaningful slippage.<ref>https://tadable.com/7-ways-to-reduce-slippage-when-trading-thin-crypto-markets/</ref>

== 3. Volume can be faked; depth is harder to fake ==

Reported volume is a favourite thing to inflate, because it is the number that gets a coin listed and ranked. '''Wash trading''' — the same party on both sides — manufactures it cheaply.

This is not a suspicion, it is a measured finding. Cong, Li, Tang and Yang examined 29 centralised exchanges and found that on the '''unregulated''' ones, fake volume averaged '''over 70% of reported volume'''.<ref>https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w30783/w30783.pdf</ref> The method is statistical rather than accusatory: regulated exchanges show the trade-size and first-significant-digit distributions you see throughout finance and nature, while unregulated ones show '''abnormal''' ones. The same authors report that exchanges listed on CoinMarketCap contained '''over 99%''' fake volume on the sample examined.

Two honest limits. The technique '''infers''' wash trading from statistical regularities and cannot prove any particular trade was fake or name who controlled the accounts; the stronger evidence comes from work using leaked internal exchange records. And the figures are from a specific sample and period — the finding to carry forward is the '''order of magnitude and the regulated/unregulated split''', not a precise percentage for any venue today.

The check is consistency: volume and depth should be of a sane relative size. A venue reporting '''$2B of daily volume with only $200k of depth within 2%''' is reporting something incoherent.<ref>https://coinbureau.com/guides/low-liquidity-crypto-indicators</ref> Liquidity is also '''fragmented''' across venues and pairs, so an aggregate figure can look healthy while the one book you are actually trading on is thin.<ref>https://www.chiliz.com/understanding-crypto-liquidity-market-depth-slippage-and-volatility-explained/</ref>

And depth is not a promise. In a fast market the displayed orders '''leave''' — which is exactly when a stop-loss turns into a market order and takes the worst fill of its life.<ref>https://tadable.com/7-ways-to-reduce-slippage-when-trading-thin-crypto-markets/</ref>

== 4. How volume actually arrives ==

Volume is not summoned by announcements. It arrives in a fairly predictable order, and each step is a thing somebody has to build or do.

# '''A market has to exist at all.''' Two-sided, with a bid and an ask. On an automated market maker like [[KulaSwap and the DEX Lineage|KulaSwap]] this means somebody has to supply both sides of a pair as liquidity. Until then there is no price — only an opinion.
# '''Depth has to be deep enough to be worth crossing.''' With a shallow pool, the first buyer moves the price so far that the second buyer is paying a silly number and stays away. Depth is what makes the second trade attractive.
# '''A reason to trade has to exist.''' Someone needs the coin for something, or believes somebody else soon will. See [[Utilities and Sinks]].
# '''Then volume compounds.''' Trades make the price look real, a real-looking price attracts more orders, more orders deepen the book, a deeper book permits larger trades. This is the flywheel, and it only spins after the first three.

This is why an AMM pool is seeded before anyone is asking for it, and why liquidity provision is rewarded: it is paying for step 2 so step 4 becomes possible. Under an AMM the mechanics are precise — the reserves ''are'' the depth, and a swap's slippage is a function of its size against those reserves.

== 5. Reading a thin market honestly ==

If you are looking at a small token anywhere, including ours:

* Look at '''depth near the mid''', not the headline cap.
* Compare the '''best bid''' to the '''best ask''' — if they are orders of magnitude apart, there is no market, there are two opinions.
* Check whether volume and depth are '''consistent''' with each other.
* Ask what the token is '''for''', because in a thin market utility is the only thing that brings a second buyer.

A thin book is a normal, expected stage for a young asset. The error is not the thinness — it is quoting a market cap off it as though the whole supply could clear at that price.

== Not investment advice ==

This page explains market structure. It is '''not''' a trading strategy, '''not''' a prediction, and '''not''' a suggestion to buy or sell. The percentage rules of thumb quoted are from trading-education sources and are heuristics, not standards.

== Coverage ==
Covers the spread/depth/slippage distinction, why volume is the weakest of the three and how it is faked, order-size heuristics against book depth, the four-step sequence by which volume actually arrives, and how to read a thin market honestly. Cites the CURE spread from the Matrix page as the worked local example. Gives no trading strategy and predicts no prices.
